q: What is required for two functions in the same scope to be overloaded?
opts: Same name but different parameter lists
Same name and same parameters but different return types
Different names but the same parameters
Same name but defined in different files only
ansText: Same name but different parameter lists
expl: Overloading = same function name, different number or types of parameters. The compiler picks the right one from the arguments.
others: Return type alone (B) can never distinguish overloads.

q: In public inheritance, what do the public members of the base class become in the derived class?
expl: Public inheritance keeps public members public and protected members protected. (Private inheritance would demote them - read the inheritance type carefully.)

q: Which type of inheritance has a class derived from two or more base classes?
expl: Multiple inheritance: class Professor : public Teacher, public Researcher - two or more direct base classes.
others: Multilevel = a chain (A->B->C); hierarchical = one base, many derived.

q: Where can a protected member of a base class be accessed?
opts: Within the base class and its derived classes
ansText: Within the base class and its derived classes
expl: protected behaves like private for the outside world, but derived classes can use it directly (e.g., brand and storage in the Device/Phone program).

q: Which operator cannot be overloaded in C++?
expl: :: , . (dot), .* and sizeof can never be overloaded. + , << and [] are commonly overloaded (Complex +, cout <<, array subscript).

q: Which keyword makes a base class member function eligible for dynamic binding?
expl: Declaring the base function virtual lets the call be resolved at run time based on the actual object type (needed for Employee* ->salary() in the salary program).

q: What is method overriding?
opts: A derived class giving its own definition of a base class function with the same signature
Defining two functions with the same name and different parameters
Calling a base class constructor from main()
Hiding all members of the base class
ansText: A derived class giving its own definition of a base class function with the same signature
expl: Same name, same parameters, but the derived version replaces the base version (B is overloading, not overriding).

q: Which statement about the this pointer is correct?
opts: It is a static member of every class
It stores the address of the base class
It can be used inside static member functions
It is passed implicitly to every non-static member function
ansText: It is passed implicitly to every non-static member function
expl: Every non-static member function receives this automatically. Static member functions have no this because they belong to the class, not an object (C is a classic trap).

q: In what order are constructors called when a derived class object is created?
opts: Derived class first, then base class
Only the derived class constructor is called
Base class first, then derived class
ansText: Base class first, then derived class
expl: The base part must exist before the derived part builds on it. Destructors run in exactly the reverse order (derived first).

q: A class becomes abstract in C++ when it contains at least one:
expl: A pure virtual function ( virtual double fee(double) = 0; ) has no body in the base class, so objects of that class cannot be created - the class is abstract.

q: What is a concrete class?
opts: A class with at least one pure virtual function
A class that implements all its functions and can be instantiated
A class that cannot have any objects
A class that has only static members
ansText: A class that implements all its functions and can be instantiated
expl: Concrete = the opposite of abstract: every pure virtual function is implemented, so objects can be created (CardPayment and UpiPayment in the Payment program).

q: When is the function to be called decided in dynamic binding?
expl: With virtual functions through a base pointer, the actual function is chosen while the program runs, using the real object type.
others: Compile-time decision = static binding (normal function calls, overloading).

q: Why should the destructor of a base class be declared virtual?
opts: To prevent the class from being inherited
To make the destructor run faster
So that deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls the derived destructor
ansText: So that deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls the derived destructor
expl: With virtual ~Payment(), delete p (p is Payment*) first runs ~CardPayment(), then ~Payment(). Without virtual, only the base destructor would run - a memory-leak trap.

q: Which keyword is used to raise an exception in C++?
expl: throw 0; or throw string("...") raises the exception; try wraps the risky code; catch receives the thrown value. There is no 'raise' keyword in C++.
